title: Yuma County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Yuma County wells have a 233 ft median depth and 15 gpm median yield. See local drilling costs, water levels, and well risks before you buy land.
h1: Water wells in Yuma County, Colorado
intro_html:
Yuma County sits over the Ogallala and other High Plains aquifers, with a long history of irrigation, stock, and domestic wells. The records here are deep enough to give you a realistic idea of how far you’ll drill, how much water you’ll likely get, and what that means for cost and risk on a specific parcel.

I’ll walk through typical depths, yields, water level trends, drilling activity, and what to watch for before you close on land or start building.

sections.heading: Typical well depth in Yuma County
sections.html:
Across 7,653 wells with a reported total depth, the median depth in Yuma County is 233 feet. The middle half of wells run from 140 to 303 feet, and only 16% are under 100 feet. About 54% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and another 30% are between 300 and 600 feet. There are very deep outliers, with the deepest at 3,650 feet, but those are not the norm.

For a new domestic or stock well, a driller is probably going to bid assuming something near that 233-foot median, but they’ll look closely at nearby wells and which aquifer they’re set in before giving you a firm estimate.

sections.heading: How much water Yuma County wells produce
sections.html:
Yields are generally solid here. From 2,828 wells reporting a pump test, the median yield is 15 gallons per minute. The middle half fall between 10 and 50 gpm. Wells under 1 gpm are recorded as 0%, and only 2% fall between 1 and 5 gpm.

Most of the production is better than that: 29% of wells land in the 5 to 15 gpm range, while 69% report 15 gpm or more. That’s enough for a typical exempt household well and small-scale stock or lawn use, assuming your permit allows it. Still, you should never assume your specific hole will match the median; local geology and how the well is completed matter a lot.

sections.heading: Water table depth and long-term trend
sections.html:
Static water levels are reported on 556 wells, with a median depth to water of 121 feet and a middle half from 72 to 180 feet. That gives you a rough idea of how far you’ll lower a pump below the water level to keep it submerged.

The decade data tell an important story. Median depth to water was about 145 feet in the 1950s, then shallowed to 91–105 feet through the 1960s–1990s. Since then, the water level has been deeper: about 121 feet in the 2000s, 142 feet in the 2010s, and 156 feet in the 2020s. That’s a clear downward trend in the water table in recent decades, which is something to factor into pump setting and long-term planning.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling wells here and for what
sections.html:
Yuma County has 12,235 wells in the state records, with 5,510 recorded as constructed. Use is heavily agricultural and rural: about 41% are stock wells, 38% irrigation, and 28% domestic or household, with another 2% for monitoring.

Drilling has been steady for decades. Permits ramped up from 183 in the 1950s to 1,565 in the 1970s, then stayed active: 760 in the 1980s, 1,228 in the 1990s, 1,085 in the 2000s, 816 in the 2010s, and 371 so far in the 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2025. The most active drillers in the records are Wellstone Industries Dba Twiss & Wilson Drilling Inc (Twiss, Raymond L.) with 1,814 wells, Burgess Well Company Inc. with 435, and Schaal Drilling Co. with 390.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Yuma County
sections.html:
The ground here is mainly alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. The going drilling rate in this setting runs about $35 to $55 per foot. At the county’s 233-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole alone roughly in the $8,200 to $12,800 range.

Once you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, a typical finished domestic well at that median depth runs about $14,200 to $24,800. If your site ends up closer to the upper end of the common range, say in the 300–600 foot bracket where 30% of wells fall, your total will scale up from there. Always base your budget on nearby well logs, not just the county median.

sections.heading: Local risks: low yield, quality, and site layout
sections.html:
On the yield side, the data are encouraging: 0% of reported wells are under 1 gpm, and only 2% are between 1 and 5 gpm. Still, there are very deep wells here, up to 3,650 feet, which tells you that in some spots it can take a lot of drilling to hit a usable zone.

Water quality needs attention. There are 74 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site mapped within about 10 miles in the county. Before you buy, plan on a full lab test panel on any existing well and pay attention to where the septic system will go. Keep adequate separation between well, septic, and any corrals or chemical storage.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in Yuma County
sections.html:
Most wells here are set in an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer (7,831 wells) or the Ogallala (4,138 wells), with another 124 in the broader High Plains Aquifer. Each behaves a little differently, so pull the nearby well permits and completion reports before committing to a lot, especially outside Yuma, Wray, Joes, Eckley, Kirk, Vernon, Idalia, or Laird.

Look for nearby wells with depths and yields similar to the county medians of 233 feet and 15 gpm. Ask how recently static water levels were measured, given the deepening trend since the 1990s. If there is no existing well, write a drilling allowance and a minimum yield requirement into your purchase contract so you’re not stuck with an underperforming hole.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Yuma County, Colorado?
faq.a: Based on 7,653 wells with reported depths, the median well in Yuma County is about 233 feet deep. The middle half of wells range from 140 to 303 feet. Around 16% of wells are shallower than 100 feet, 54% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and 30% run 300 to 600 feet. The deepest recorded well in the county reaches 3,650 feet, but that is an outlier, not typical for domestic wells.

faq.q: How much water do Yuma County wells usually produce?
faq.a: From 2,828 wells with reported pump tests, the median yield in Yuma County is 15 gallons per minute. The middle half of wells fall between 10 and 50 gpm. Very low producers are uncommon in the data: 0% are under 1 gpm and 2% are between 1 and 5 gpm. About 29% are in the 5–15 gpm range, and 69% report 15 gpm or more, which is usually sufficient for household use.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Yuma County, Colorado?
faq.a: Static water level records show a long-term deepening of the water table in recent decades. Median depth to water was about 145 feet in the 1950s, then shallowed into the 91–105 foot range through the 1960s–1990s. Since 2000 it has deepened again, to about 121 feet in the 2000s, 142 feet in the 2010s, and 156 feet in the 2020s. That trend means wells may need deeper pumps and more careful long-term planning.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a water well in Yuma County?
faq.a: In Yuma County’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, drilling typically runs about $35 to $55 per foot. At the county’s 233-foot median depth, the borehole alone comes out roughly $8,200 to $12,800. A complete domestic well with casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical usually totals around $14,200 to $24,800 at that median depth. Deeper wells in the 300–600 foot range will scale up from these figures.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Yuma County, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. Yuma County has 74 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site within about 10 miles, so water quality should never be assumed. Before drinking from an existing well, have it tested by a certified lab for bacteria, nitrates, and relevant chemicals. For a new well, test as soon as it is completed and again after the system has been in use for a while.
